Remigius of Lyon
rə-mij'ee-əs əv lē-ōn'
n. (Remigius, archbishop of Lyon 852–875, who presided over the synod of Valence in 855)
Latin Remigius, from remex, an oarsman.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Remigius succeeded Amolo at Lyon in 852 and made his church the chief opponent of Hincmar's articles of Quierzy. A treatise issued in the name of the church of Lyon, usually attributed to him, answered three letters circulated by Hincmar's party and argued that Gottschalk had been condemned unjustly and punished cruelly. In January 855 Remigius presided with Agilmar of Vienne and Ebbo of Grenoble over the synod of Valence. Its canons confessed the predestination of the elect to life, and the predestination of the wicked to death, while insisting that in the condemnation of the wicked their own desert precedes God's just judgment, and that God does not predestine any man to sin. Valence rejected the four articles of Quierzy and dismissed the nineteen propositions of John Scotus Eriugena with contempt as Scots porridge. Remigius sat again at the councils of Langres and Savonnieres in 859 and at Tusey in 860, where an ambiguous compromise ended the quarrel without deciding it. He held Paul's line: “Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council.

expand to see more

CAN'ON, n. A law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.

COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline in the church.

DESERT', n. That which gives a right to reward or demands punishment; merit or demerit.

Modern Corruption

The synod of Valence: double predestination confessed, with the sinner's own guilt kept in view.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The canons of Valence are a model of the care the doctrine requires, and the misuse of the doctrine they guard against is the one its enemies still allege: that to confess reprobation is to make God the author of sin. Valence said the opposite in so many words. Election is not of works, “that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11); reprobation finds the sinner already guilty.

The principle to recover is that Christ's own intercession is particular. “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (John 17:9). Lyon saw that a redemption Christ does not plead for is not the redemption the Scriptures describe, and that the church owes the persecuted Gottschalk an apology Hincmar never offered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek skleruno (G4645), to harden; prothesis (G4286), purpose; haireomai (G138), to choose.

Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; Romans 9:18.

Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting forth, purpose; Romans 9:11.

Greek erotao (G2065) — to ask, pray; John 17:9.

Greek haireomai (G138) — to take for oneself, choose; 2 Thessalonians 2:13.

Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification; 2 Thessalonians 2:13.

Usage

"“whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18) — the sovereignty Valence confessed."

"“I pray not for the world” (John 17:9) — a particular intercession."

"“chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit” (2Th 2:13) — the means joined to the end."
